patient.chief_complaint: Bilateral eyelid swelling and double vision with abnormal eye movements
patient.hpi:
A 52-year-old African American woman with hypertension presented to the neurology ward with a 2-week history of bilateral eyelid swelling, double vision, and abnormal eye movements. She reported blurred vision that fluctuated in severity, with the right eye appearing more affected. She initially noticed left upper eyelid swelling and heaviness, followed by diplopia on rightward gaze. She denied fever, photophobia, jaw or swallowing difficulty, limb weakness, numbness, or gait disturbance. She had no preceding infections, vaccinations, or recent travel. She declined the ice pack test initially as she was concerned it would cause pain.

On examination, swelling of the left upper eyelid was prominent. Extraocular movement testing revealed the right eye failed to move fully in the horizontal plane, and the left eye had impaired adduction with preserved abduction, producing a pattern consistent with pseudo-internuclear ophthalmoplegia (pseudo-INO). The left upper eyelid was ptotic. On upgaze, the left eye failed to fully elevate. A Cogan lid twitch sign was elicited in the left eye on downgaze and return to primary position. Visual acuity and fundoscopy were normal. The rest of the neurological examination was unremarkable.

Given the pseudo-INO pattern, the neurology team initially considered a brainstem structural lesion or TIA and ordered urgent imaging. CT of the orbits, MRI of the brain, MRA, and MRV were all unremarkable. Following normal imaging, the pattern of fatigable, asymmetric ocular motor signs prompted consideration of myasthenia gravis.
pmh: No prior neurological or autoimmune diagnosis

family_history: Mother had hypertension; no family history of autoimmune or neuromuscular disease

social_history.note: Elementary school teacher; non-smoker; non-drinker; married; three children; active prior to symptom onset

physical_exam.general: Alert, well-appearing woman; left upper eyelid swelling and ptosis evident
physical_exam.neurological: Left upper eyelid ptosis with periorbital swelling. Cogan lid twitch positive (left). Right eye: limited horizontal movement in both directions. Left eye: impaired adduction with preserved abduction (pseudo-INO pattern). Left eye failure to fully elevate on upgaze. No nystagmus. Visual acuity 20/20 bilaterally. Pupils equal and reactive. No proptosis. No pain on eye movement. Motor exam 5/5 all limbs. Reflexes 2+ symmetric. Sensation intact. Coordination normal. No fasciculations.
physical_exam.cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm; no murmurs

differential.key_features: Normal brain MRI/MRA/DWI; no basilar territory infarct; fatigable ocular signs argue against fixed vascular deficit
No ataxia, no areflexia; anti-GQ1b negative; no preceding illness; not acute progressive

differential.diagnosis: Orbital cellulitis or cavernous sinus thrombosis
differential.key_features: No fever, no chemosis, no proptosis; MRI normal including cavernous sinus; no thrombosis on MRV
differential.distinguishing_test: Brain MRI/MRV (normal), lack of inflammatory signs

differential.key_features: Normal TSH; no proptosis, no lid retraction; ptosis (not retraction); normal orbital muscles on MRI

optimal_actions.action: Brain MRI with DWI, MRA, and MRV to exclude structural brainstem lesion and vascular etiology
AChR antibody testing after normal imaging confirms MG etiology
Anti-GQ1b antibody to exclude Miller-Fisher syndrome
Initiate pyridostigmine for symptom management and add prednisone for immunosuppression

critical_actions: Obtain brain MRI/DWI urgently to exclude brainstem TIA (given hypertension + pseudo-INO pattern)
Recognize Cogan lid twitch as highly specific sign of MG
Order AChR antibody after normal imaging
CT chest for thymoma screening in all newly diagnosed MG
Assess NIF and FVC — even in ocular MG, monitor for progression to generalized disease
contraindicated_actions: Do not initiate anticoagulation without confirmed ischemic etiology
Do not prescribe fluoroquinolones or aminoglycosides for any concurrent infection
Do not miss the anti-GQ1b test if Miller-Fisher syndrome remains on differential
key_reasoning_points: Pseudo-INO without brainstem structural correlate on MRI is a classic presentation of ocular MG
Cogan lid twitch sign is 98% specific for MG when present
Normal brain MRI/DWI is the key that redirects from vascular to neuromuscular etiology
AChR antibody 7.6 nmol/L is strongly positive and diagnostic
Anti-GQ1b negative effectively excludes Miller-Fisher syndrome
Ocular MG without limb or respiratory involvement: current pyridostigmine + prednisone strategy

red_herrings.why_misleading: Pseudo-INO with bilateral horizontal restriction mimics true INO from brainstem lesion
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: True INO requires structural MLF lesion; normal brain MRI and fatigable nature confirm MG etiology

red_herrings.why_misleading: Eyelid swelling + restricted eye movement can resemble orbital cellulitis
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: No fever, no chemosis, no proptosis, normal orbital MRI — orbital infection excluded

red_herrings.why_misleading: Hypertension raises pre-test probability for TIA/stroke as cause of focal neurological signs
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Normal MRI/MRA excludes vascular etiology; MG is the diagnosis regardless of vascular risk factors

metadata.condition_name: Ocular myasthenia gravis with pseudo-INO pattern
metadata.difficulty_description: Straightforward: imaging excludes structural cause; Cogan lid twitch and AChR antibody confirm MG; pseudo-INO in MG is a classic presentation

mri.impression: Normal brain MRI/MRA/MRV; no brainstem lesion; normal MLF; no orbital pathology — pseudo-INO pattern unexplained by imaging. Clinical correlation recommended.

output.report:
LITERATURE SEARCH: Ocular MG — Treatment and Progression

KEY FINDINGS:
1. PYRIDOSTIGMINE: First-line symptomatic treatment; 60 mg q4-6h; particularly effective for ptosis
2. GENERALIZATION RISK: ~50% of purely ocular MG generalizes within 2 years; AChR antibody presence increases this risk
3. IMMUNOSUPPRESSION: Prednisone recommended for ocular MG not controlled by pyridostigmine; reduces generalization risk
4. THYMECTOMY: Controversial for isolated ocular MG; MGTX trial included only generalized MG patients
5. FOLLOW-UP: NIF and FVC monitoring at each visit; prompt evaluation if symptoms change

CONCLUSION: Initiate pyridostigmine and prednisone (with monitoring); follow-up in 3 months; educate regarding generalization risk.
output.summary: Pyridostigmine first-line; 50% generalization risk within 2 years in AChR+ ocular MG; immunosuppression reduces progression

output.report:
DRUG INTERACTION REVIEW — AMLODIPINE AND MG

Query: Calcium channel blocker (amlodipine) safety in MG

FINDINGS:
  AMLODIPINE (calcium channel blocker):
  - Calcium channel blockers may impair neuromuscular transmission (calcium required for ACh vesicle release)
  - Case reports of CCB-related MG exacerbation exist but are rare
  - Clinical significance of amlodipine at standard doses is low for most MG patients
  - If worsening occurs, discuss with cardiology regarding alternative antihypertensive (e.g., ACE inhibitor)

CONCLUSION: Amlodipine is generally safe at standard doses in MG. Hydrochlorothiazide has no MG interactions. Continue current antihypertensive regimen with clinical monitoring.
output.summary: Amlodipine: low MG risk at standard doses; continue with monitoring; HCTZ has no MG interaction
